title: Mahala 1, mahala 5
hook: every Guru signed as Nanak; the heading mahala with a number tells you which Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, bani, and your line: many voices, one guru. Did you listen properly to a voice you usually skip past? Today, how you can tell the Gurus' voices apart, when they all use the same name. Day two hundred thirty-four.

Here's a puzzle. You're reading the Granth, and you reach the last line of a hymn. It says: Nanak says this. Easy, you think, Guru Nanak wrote it. You turn the page, and the next hymn also ends with Nanak. And the next. But some of these hymns praise the pool of Guru Ram Das, a pool dug long after Guru Nanak was gone. They speak of things Guru Nanak never lived to see. So who's writing? Every one of these poets signs with the same name. Today you'll learn the little heading that solves the puzzle, and why the name never changes.
screen: `NANAK SAYS, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `BUT LONG AFTER HIM?` → `WHO IS WRITING?`

segments.voice: Look at the top of a hymn, not the bottom. There you'll find a heading: first the raga, then a word and a number. Sri Rag, mahala 1. Gauri, mahala 3. Asa, mahala 5. Today's word is mahala. The number tells you which Guru. Mahala 1 is Guru Nanak. Mahala 2, Guru Angad. Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das. Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das. Mahala 5, Guru Arjan, who compiled the book. And mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur, whose hymns were added later. There's no run of mahala 10 hymns: tradition says Guru Gobind Singh added his father's hymns, then gave the Guruship to the Granth itself, and his own writings are collected elsewhere. What does mahala mean? Its meaning is debated. One common reading takes it from mahal, a house or dwelling: the first body, the fifth body. That fits the heart of the matter. Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light, one jot, passing from one to the next, the way one lamp lights another. The Granth itself says it, in the ballad of Satta and Balwand: the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body has changed. That's why every Guru signs as Nanak. It isn't borrowing a famous name. It's saying the same light is speaking. The Bhagats, by contrast, sign with their own names: Kabir says, Ravidas says, Farid says. So the bottom line tells you whether it's the Nanak light speaking, and the heading tells you through which Guru. Many voices, one Guru, and now you can read the map.
screen: `THE HEADING: A RAGA AND A NUMBER.` · `MAHALA 1 IS NANAK, 5 IS ARJAN.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP TO LAMP.` · `THE BHAGATS SIGN THEIR OWN NAMES.` · then, large: `EVERY GURU SIGNS AS NANAK.`

segments.voice: Picture a row of oil lamps in a dark room. One is lit. Watch someone tip a second lamp toward it until the wick catches. Then a third from the second. Then a fourth. The flame moves down the row, and it's the same flame. Breathe slowly as you watch it pass. With each breath out, see one more lamp catch. Let the room fill with light, one lamp at a time. The bell holds the time.
Mahala. The heading word with a number that tells you which Guru wrote a hymn, mahala 1 for Guru Nanak, mahala 5 for Guru Arjan, because every Guru signs as Nanak.
Your line: every guru signs as nanak. Today, if you can, open the Granth or an online reader and find one mahala heading. Read the number, and name the Guru. Day two hundred thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 234 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HUKAM: LIVING IN THE ORDER.`

howItsDone: When a hymn is read in the gurdwara, the reader often announces its heading, such as Sorath mahala 5, so listeners know which Guru's words they are hearing; the hymn itself ends with the name Nanak.

fork.setup: a hymn ends: Nanak says. its heading reads Asa, mahala 5. who wrote it?
fork.reveal: mahala 5 is Guru Arjan. he signs as Nanak because Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light, passed lamp to lamp.

original.note: Gurmukhi: mahala, the heading word followed by a number that tells which Guru wrote a hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: mahala means chapter.
what it means: a heading with a number naming the Guru, because all the Gurus sign as Nanak, one light in many lamps.
what a scholar hears: the word's origin is debated, often read as dwelling or body from mahal; the headings run mahala 1 to 5 and 9.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib (raga headings, e.g. Sri Rag Mahala 1, Ang 14)

Guru Granth Sahib (Bhagat bani signatures, e.g. Kabir)

notes: Guru Nanak's death given as 1539; confirm.

Hook says later hymns mention Amritsar and the digging of the pool; this is widely taught (e.g. Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan hymns on Ramdaspur and the sarovar) but no specific hymn is cited. Confirm or soften.
The meaning of mahala is presented as debated, with the 'dwelling/body' reading given as common; confirm.
Guru Gobind Singh's writings 'kept elsewhere' (the Dasam Granth) left unnamed to avoid its debates; confirm.

Editor review: cut Guru Nanak's death year and the unsourced 'city of Amritsar' claim; the hook now names Guru Ram Das's pool (confirm a hymn, e.g. Sorath Mahala 5 on Ramdas sarovar, around Ang 623-625); 'no mahala 10' softened to 'no run of mahala 10 hymns', since a salok near the end (Ang 1429, salok 54) is attributed by some to Guru Gobind Singh; the meaning of mahala now 'debated, one common reading' instead of 'many read'; the one-light teaching now cites Satta and Balwand's Var (Ang 966, paraphrased).
